title: UNIT 3: INDUSTRIAL CHEMISTRY
notes:
✓ Industrial chemistry → The branch of chemistry concerned with the large-scale production of useful substances and materials.
It involves the conversion of natural resources and raw materials into valuable products through chemical and physical processes.

✓ Industrial chemistry connects chemistry with engineering, economics, agriculture, energy, environmental protection, and everyday life.

title: 3.1 Introduction
notes:
✓ Industrial chemistry → The manufacture of chemicals and useful materials on a large scale.

✓ Industrial processes use chemical reactions, separation methods, heating, cooling, pressure, catalysts, and other techniques to convert raw materials into valuable products.

◆ EXAMPLES OF INDUSTRIAL CHEMICAL PRODUCTS
✓ Ammonia.
✓ Nitric acid.
✓ Sulfuric acid.
✓ Sodium carbonate.
✓ Sodium hydroxide.
✓ Fertilizers.
✓ Pesticides.
✓ Glass.
✓ Cement.
✓ Soap.
✓ Detergents.
✓ Ethanol.
✓ Food products.

✓ A successful industrial process should produce a useful product efficiently, safely, economically, and with minimum environmental damage.

◆ IMPORTANT FACTORS
✓ Availability and cost of raw materials.
✓ Energy requirements.
✓ Temperature and pressure.
✓ Rate of reaction.
✓ Use of catalysts.
✓ Product yield and purity.
✓ Transportation and storage.
✓ Waste treatment and environmental protection.
✓ Safety of workers and surrounding communities.

title: 3.2 Natural Resources and Industry
notes:
✓ Natural resources → Materials obtained directly or indirectly from nature and used as sources of raw materials, energy, or other useful products.

✓ Industries depend heavily on natural resources for manufacturing.

◆ TYPES OF NATURAL RESOURCES
✓ Renewable resources → Resources that can be replenished naturally over a relatively short period.
Examples → Agricultural crops, forests, and some biological materials.

✓ Non-renewable resources → Resources that occur in limited amounts and may take millions of years to form.
Examples → Minerals, petroleum, natural gas, and coal.

✓ Industries transform these resources into products that are useful to society.

◆ EXAMPLES
Limestone → Cement production.
Agricultural products → Food processing.
Minerals → Metals and other chemical products.

✓ Sustainable use of resources is important because excessive extraction can lead to depletion, pollution, soil degradation, deforestation, and other environmental problems.

title: 3.2.1 Natural Resources (Raw Materials)
notes:
✓ Raw materials → Substances used as starting materials in industrial production.
They may come from mineral, biological, agricultural, or fossil-fuel sources.

◆ IMPORTANT CATEGORIES OF RAW MATERIALS
✓ Mineral resources → Limestone, salt, sulfur-containing minerals, and metal ores.
✓ Agricultural resources → Sugarcane, grains, oilseeds, cotton, and animal products.
✓ Forest resources → Wood and cellulose.
✓ Fossil resources → Petroleum, natural gas, and coal.
✓ Atmospheric resources → Nitrogen and oxygen from air.
✓ Water → Widely used as a solvent, reactant, coolant, and cleaning medium.

✓ The suitability of a raw material depends on its availability, composition, purity, cost, transportation requirements, and processing requirements.

◆ EXAMPLES
Atmospheric nitrogen → Important raw material for ammonia production.
Limestone → Important raw material for cement and sodium carbonate production.

✓ Industries must use raw materials efficiently and minimize unnecessary losses and waste.

title: 3.2.2 Industry
notes:
✓ Industry → An organized system in which raw materials, labor, energy, technology, equipment, and capital are combined to produce useful goods or services.

◆ CLASSIFICATION OF INDUSTRIES
✓ Manufacturing industries → Convert raw materials into finished or semi-finished products.
✓ Extractive industries → Obtain resources directly from nature.
✓ Processing industries → Transform raw materials into more useful forms.

◆ GENERAL INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION PROCESS
Raw materials → Processing → Chemical/physical transformation → Separation and purification → Product → Packaging and distribution

◆ IMPORTANT INDUSTRIAL CONSIDERATIONS
✓ Production capacity.
✓ Quality control.
✓ Energy efficiency.
✓ Cost.
✓ Safety.
✓ Environmental impact.
✓ Waste management.

✓ Large-scale chemical manufacturing often uses continuous processes in which raw materials are continuously supplied and products are continuously removed.
✓ Other processes may operate in batches.

title: 3.3 Manufacturing of Valuable Products/Chemicals
notes:
✓ Industrial chemical manufacturing → The conversion of raw materials into useful chemicals through carefully controlled physical and chemical processes.

◆ IMPORTANT INDUSTRIAL CHEMICALS
✓ Ammonia.
✓ Nitric acid.
✓ Sulfuric acid.
✓ Fertilizers.
✓ Pesticides.
✓ Sodium carbonate.
✓ Sodium hydroxide.

◆ COMMON STAGES OF INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTION
◆ 1. Preparation of raw materials.
◆ 2. Chemical reaction or transformation.
◆ 3. Separation of products from unreacted materials.
◆ 4. Purification and concentration.
◆ 5. Recycling of useful reactants.
◆ 6. Storage and packaging.

✓ Industrial processes are designed to maximize useful product formation while minimizing energy consumption, waste, and production costs.

✓ Temperature, pressure, concentration, catalysts, reaction rate, equilibrium, and heat transfer are important in designing and operating chemical plants.

title: 3.3.1 Ammonia (NH₃)
notes:
✓ Ammonia → An important industrial chemical used mainly in the manufacture of fertilizers.
It is also used in the production of nitric acid, explosives, cleaning products, refrigerants, and various nitrogen-containing chemicals.

◆ HABER PROCESS
✓ Nitrogen is obtained mainly from air, while hydrogen can be obtained from natural gas or other hydrogen-containing sources.

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)    ΔH < 0

✓ The reaction is reversible and exothermic.

◆ IMPORTANT CONDITIONS
✓ Temperature → Approximately 450°C.
✓ Pressure → High pressure, commonly around 200 atm in conventional descriptions.
✓ Catalyst → Finely divided iron with suitable promoters.

✓ High pressure favors ammonia formation because the number of gas molecules decreases from four moles to two moles.
✓ A moderately high temperature is used as a compromise between reaction rate and equilibrium yield.

✓ Because the reaction is reversible, the ammonia formed is separated by cooling and liquefaction, while unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.

✓ The Haber process is extremely important because it provides a major source of fixed nitrogen for fertilizer production.

title: 3.3.1.1 Haber Process and Industrial Conditions
notes:
✓ The Haber process illustrates how equilibrium principles are applied to industrial chemistry.

◆ REACTION
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat

◆ EFFECT OF PRESSURE
✓ There are four moles of gaseous reactants but only two moles of gaseous product.
→ Increasing pressure favors ammonia formation.
✓ Extremely high pressures require expensive equipment and increase operating costs, so an economically practical pressure is selected.

◆ EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE
✓ The forward reaction is exothermic, so lower temperature favors ammonia equilibrium yield.
✓ Very low temperature makes the reaction too slow.
→ A compromise temperature is therefore used.

◆ ROLE OF CATALYST
✓ The iron catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached.
✓ It does not change the equilibrium position or the final equilibrium yield.

◆ RECYCLING
✓ Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back into the reactor to improve overall efficiency and reduce waste.

title: 3.3.2 Nitric Acid
notes:
✓ Nitric acid, HNO₃ → A strong acid and an important industrial chemical.
It is widely used in fertilizer production, explosives, metal treatment, and the manufacture of many nitrogen-containing chemicals.

◆ OSTWALD PROCESS
✓ Nitric acid is mainly produced industrially using ammonia as the starting material.

◆ STEP 1: OXIDATION OF AMMONIA
✓ Ammonia is oxidized by oxygen in the presence of a platinum-rhodium catalyst at high temperature:
4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O

◆ STEP 2: OXIDATION OF NITRIC OXIDE
2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂

◆ STEP 3: ABSORPTION OF NITROGEN DIOXIDE
3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO

✓ The nitric oxide formed can be recycled and oxidized again.

✓ The Ostwald process demonstrates the importance of catalysts, controlled oxidation, gas absorption, and recycling in industrial chemistry.

title: 3.3.3 Nitrogen-Based Fertilizers
notes:
✓ Nitrogen-based fertilizers → Substances that supply plants with nitrogen, an essential nutrient required for the formation of proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll, and other important biological compounds.

✓ Ammonia is a major starting material for many nitrogen fertilizers.

◆ IMPORTANT NITROGEN FERTILIZERS
✓ Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃.
✓ Ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄.
✓ Urea, CO(NH₂)₂.
✓ Ammonium phosphate fertilizers.

◆ AMMONIUM NITRATE PRODUCTION
NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃

✓ Ammonium nitrate can be produced by neutralizing nitric acid with ammonia.

✓ Urea is another important nitrogen fertilizer and can be manufactured from ammonia and carbon dioxide through intermediate ammonium compounds.

✓ Fertilizers improve crop growth by supplying nutrients that may be deficient in soil.
✓ Excessive fertilizer use can cause environmental problems such as water pollution, eutrophication, and soil nutrient imbalance.

✓ Efficient fertilizer use requires applying the correct nutrient, amount, timing, and placement according to crop and soil requirements.

title: 3.3.4 Sulfuric Acid
notes:
✓ Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄ → One of the most important industrial chemicals.
It is used in fertilizer production, petroleum refining, metal processing, batteries, chemical manufacturing, and many other industries.

◆ CONTACT PROCESS

◆ STEP 1: PRODUCTION OF SULFUR DIOXIDE
S + O₂ → SO₂

✓ Sulfur dioxide may also be obtained by roasting sulfide ores.

◆ STEP 2: OXIDATION OF SULFUR DIOXIDE
2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃

✓ This reaction is exothermic and is carried out in the presence of a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, V₂O₅, at about 450°C.

◆ STEP 3: ABSORPTION OF SULFUR TRIOXIDE
✓ Sulfur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum rather than being directly absorbed in water.

SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇

✓ The oleum is then diluted with water:
H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

✓ Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive and must be handled carefully.

title: 3.3.5 Some Common Pesticides and Herbicides
notes:
✓ Pesticides → Substances used to control organisms that damage crops, stored products, animals, or human health.
✓ Herbicides → Pesticides specifically used to control unwanted plants or weeds.

◆ MAJOR PESTICIDE CATEGORIES
✓ Insecticides → Control insects.
✓ Herbicides → Control weeds.
✓ Fungicides → Control fungal diseases.
✓ Rodenticides → Control rodents.

✓ Herbicides may be selective, affecting particular weeds while causing less damage to crops, or non-selective, affecting a broad range of plants.

◆ EXAMPLES OF HERBICIDES
✓ Glyphosate.
✓ 2,4-D.
✓ Atrazine.

✓ Different pesticides have different chemical structures, modes of action, persistence, and environmental effects.

✓ Pesticides can improve agricultural productivity, but improper or excessive use can contaminate soil and water, affect non-target organisms, and contribute to health and environmental risks.

✓ Safe pesticide use requires correct selection, dosage, application method, storage, protective equipment, and proper disposal.

title: 3.3.6 Sodium Carbonate (Na₂CO₃)
notes:
✓ Sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ → An important industrial chemical commonly known as soda ash.
It is used in glass manufacturing, detergents, water treatment, paper production, and chemical industries.

◆ SOLVAY PROCESS
✓ A major industrial method for producing sodium carbonate.
✓ Important raw materials → Brine, limestone, and ammonia.

✓ The process involves several stages, including the production of carbon dioxide from limestone, formation of ammonium bicarbonate, precipitation of sodium bicarbonate, and heating of sodium bicarbonate.

◆ KEY REACTION
NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O

✓ Sodium bicarbonate is heated to produce sodium carbonate.

◆ LIMESTONE DECOMPOSITION
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

✓ The carbon dioxide is used in the carbonation stage, while ammonia is recovered and recycled.

✓ The Solvay process is important because recycling of ammonia reduces the amount of raw material required and improves economic efficiency.

title: 3.3.7 Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH)
notes:
✓ Sodium hydroxide, NaOH → A strong alkali widely used in industry and commonly called caustic soda.

◆ USES
✓ Soap and detergent manufacture.
✓ Paper production.
✓ Textile processing.
✓ Alumina production.
✓ Petroleum refining.
✓ Chemical manufacturing.

◆ CHLOR-ALKALI PROCESS
✓ Sodium hydroxide is mainly produced by the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride.

◆ OVERALL REACTION
2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂

◆ CATHODE
2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻

◆ ANODE
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

✓ The process produces three valuable products → Sodium hydroxide, hydrogen, and chlorine.

✓ Modern industrial cells are designed to keep the products separated because chlorine can react with sodium hydroxide under unsuitable conditions.

title: 3.4 Some Manufacturing Industries in Ethiopia
notes:
✓ Manufacturing industries in Ethiopia → Industries that transform locally available agricultural products, minerals, and other raw materials into useful goods.

✓ They contribute to employment, economic development, value addition, import substitution, and the supply of consumer and industrial products.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Glass.
✓ Ceramics.
✓ Cement.
✓ Sugar.
✓ Paper and pulp.
✓ Tanning.
✓ Food processing.
✓ Ethanol.
✓ Soap and detergent production.

✓ The availability of raw materials, energy, water, transportation, skilled labor, technology, markets, and investment strongly influences the development and location of industries.

✓ Industrial development also requires attention to waste management, pollution control, worker safety, and efficient use of natural resources.

title: 3.4.1 Glass Manufacturing
notes:
✓ Glass → An inorganic material produced by heating suitable raw materials until they form a molten or semi-molten mixture that can be shaped and cooled to produce a hard, usually transparent material.

✓ The main raw material for ordinary soda-lime glass is silica, usually supplied by sand.
✓ Other important materials include sodium carbonate and limestone.

◆ MAJOR STEPS
◆ 1. Preparation and mixing of raw materials.
◆ 2. Melting at high temperature.
◆ 3. Refining to remove bubbles and impurities.
◆ 4. Forming or shaping the molten glass.
◆ 5. Controlled cooling or annealing.
◆ 6. Finishing and inspection.

✓ Soda-lime glass is widely used for windows, bottles, containers, and other products.

✓ The controlled cooling stage is important because rapid cooling can create internal stresses that make glass more likely to break.

title: 3.4.2 Manufacturing of Ceramics
notes:
✓ Ceramics → Inorganic, non-metallic materials produced by shaping and heating natural or synthetic mineral-based raw materials.

◆ COMMON RAW MATERIALS
✓ Clay.
✓ Feldspar.
✓ Silica.
✓ Other mineral materials.

◆ GENERAL MANUFACTURING PROCESS
◆ 1. Selection and preparation of raw materials.
◆ 2. Crushing, grinding, and mixing.
◆ 3. Shaping or forming.
◆ 4. Drying.
◆ 5. Firing at high temperature.
◆ 6. Glazing when required.
◆ 7. Final inspection and finishing.

✓ During firing, physical and chemical changes occur that give ceramic products their hardness, strength, durability, and resistance to heat and chemicals.

✓ Ceramics are used for bricks, tiles, pottery, sanitary products, electrical insulators, and many construction materials.

title: 3.4.3 Cement Manufacturing
notes:
✓ Cement → A finely powdered binding material that hardens when mixed with water and is an essential component of concrete and mortar.

✓ The major raw materials for ordinary Portland cement are limestone and clay or other sources of calcium, silicon, aluminium, and iron.

◆ MAIN STAGES
◆ 1. Quarrying and crushing raw materials.
◆ 2. Grinding and mixing.
◆ 3. Heating the mixture in a rotary kiln.
◆ 4. Formation of clinker.
◆ 5. Cooling the clinker.
◆ 6. Grinding clinker with a suitable amount of gypsum.
◆ 7. Storage and packaging.

◆ LIMESTONE DECOMPOSITION
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

✓ Calcium oxide then reacts with silica, alumina, and iron-containing materials to form clinker minerals.

✓ Gypsum is added during final grinding to help control the setting time of cement.

✓ Cement production requires large amounts of energy and releases carbon dioxide, so energy efficiency and emissions reduction are important environmental considerations.

title: 3.4.4 Sugar Manufacturing
notes:
✓ Sugar manufacturing → The process of extracting sucrose from sugarcane or sugar beet and purifying and crystallizing it to obtain sugar.

◆ MAJOR STAGES OF SUGAR PRODUCTION FROM SUGARCANE
◆ 1. Harvesting and transporting sugarcane.
◆ 2. Washing and preparation.
◆ 3. Crushing or milling to extract juice.
◆ 4. Clarification of the juice.
◆ 5. Evaporation to concentrate the juice.
◆ 6. Crystallization of sugar.
◆ 7. Separation of crystals from mother liquor.
◆ 8. Drying and packaging.

✓ The extracted juice contains sucrose along with water and various impurities.
✓ Clarification removes suspended materials and other unwanted substances.
✓ The concentrated syrup is crystallized, and the sugar crystals are separated from molasses.

◆ BY-PRODUCTS
✓ Bagasse → Can be used as a fuel or as a raw material for other products.
✓ Molasses → Can be used in fermentation and ethanol production.

title: 3.4.5 Paper and Pulp
notes:
✓ Paper → Mainly produced from cellulose fibers.
✓ Wood is a major source of cellulose in many countries, while agricultural residues and recycled paper can also be used as raw materials.

◆ GENERAL PAPER MANUFACTURING PROCESS
◆ 1. Preparation of raw materials.
◆ 2. Pulping to separate cellulose fibers.
◆ 3. Washing and screening.
◆ 4. Bleaching when required.
◆ 5. Refining and mixing with additives.
◆ 6. Formation of a wet fiber sheet.
◆ 7. Pressing and drying.
◆ 8. Finishing and cutting.

✓ Pulping can be mechanical or chemical.
✓ Chemical pulping removes much of the lignin and produces cellulose-rich fibers.

✓ Paper products are widely used for writing, printing, packaging, hygiene products, and many other purposes.

✓ Recycling paper can reduce the demand for fresh raw materials and decrease waste, although recycled fibers become shorter and weaker after repeated processing.

title: 3.4.6 Tannery
notes:
✓ Tanning → The industrial process of converting animal hides and skins into leather that is more durable, resistant to decomposition, and suitable for manufacturing products.

◆ GENERAL TANNING PROCESS
◆ 1. Curing and preservation of hides.
◆ 2. Soaking to remove dirt and restore moisture.
◆ 3. Liming to remove hair and unwanted materials.
◆ 4. Fleshing and trimming.
◆ 5. Deliming and bating.
◆ 6. Pickling.
◆ 7. Tanning.
◆ 8. Dyeing and fatliquoring.
◆ 9. Drying, finishing, and polishing.

✓ Tanning can be carried out using different tanning agents.
✓ Chromium salts are widely used in modern tanning, while vegetable tannins are also used for certain types of leather.

✓ Tannery wastewater may contain organic matter, salts, sulfides, and chromium compounds depending on the process.
→ Proper wastewater treatment is essential to reduce environmental pollution.

title: 3.4.7 Food Processing and Preservation
notes:
✓ Food processing → The transformation of raw agricultural products into safe, stable, convenient, and useful food products.
✓ Food preservation → Methods used to prevent or slow microbial growth, enzymatic reactions, oxidation, and other processes that cause food spoilage.

◆ COMMON FOOD-PROCESSING METHODS
✓ Washing.
✓ Cutting.
✓ Grinding.
✓ Heating.
✓ Drying.
✓ Fermentation.
✓ Freezing.
✓ Pasteurization.
✓ Packaging.

◆ COMMON PRESERVATION METHODS
✓ Drying → Removes water needed by microorganisms.
✓ Refrigeration → Slows microbial and enzymatic activity.
✓ Freezing → Greatly slows chemical and biological reactions.
✓ Pasteurization → Uses controlled heating to reduce harmful microorganisms.
✓ Canning → Combines heat treatment with sealed packaging.
✓ Salting or curing → Reduces available water and inhibits microbial growth.
✓ Fermentation → Uses microorganisms to produce acids, alcohols, or other substances that help preserve food.

✓ Proper food processing and preservation improve shelf life, safety, quality, transportation, and availability.

title: 3.4.8 Manufacturing of Ethanol
notes:
✓ Ethanol, C₂H₅OH → An alcohol that can be produced industrially through fermentation of carbohydrate-rich materials or by hydration of ethene.

✓ In many biological production systems, agricultural materials containing sugars or starch are used.
✓ Microorganisms such as yeast convert fermentable sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

◆ FERMENTATION REACTION
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

◆ GENERAL STAGES OF ETHANOL PRODUCTION FROM BIOMASS
◆ 1. Preparation of the raw material.
◆ 2. Conversion of starch to fermentable sugars when necessary.
◆ 3. Fermentation using suitable microorganisms.
◆ 4. Separation of ethanol from the fermented mixture.
◆ 5. Distillation and purification.
◆ 6. Dehydration when high-purity ethanol is required.

◆ USES
✓ Solvent.
✓ Fuel or fuel additive.
✓ Disinfectant.
✓ Raw material in chemical manufacturing.

✓ Fermentation efficiency depends on factors such as temperature, pH, sugar concentration, microorganism type, and oxygen availability.

title: 3.4.9 Soap and Detergent
notes:
✓ Soap and detergents → Cleaning agents that help remove grease, oils, dirt, and other substances from surfaces.

◆ SOAP
✓ Soaps are generally sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids.
✓ They are commonly produced by the reaction of fats or oils with a strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide.
✓ This process is called saponification.

◆ GENERAL REACTION
Fat or oil + NaOH → Soap + Glycerol

✓ The soap molecule contains a non-polar hydrocarbon tail that interacts with grease and a polar or ionic head that interacts with water.
✓ Soap molecules can form micelles around oily materials, allowing them to be suspended in water and washed away.

◆ DETERGENTS
✓ Synthetic detergents contain surfactant molecules designed to reduce surface tension and help remove dirt and grease.
✓ Many detergents work effectively in hard water because they do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions as ordinary soaps can.

✓ Detergents may contain surfactants, builders, enzymes, fragrances, bleaching agents, and other additives depending on their intended use.

✓ Environmental considerations are important because some detergent components can contribute to water pollution and eutrophication if released in excessive amounts.

title: INDUSTRIAL CHEMISTRY — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ Industrial chemistry → Converts raw materials into useful products through controlled chemical and physical processes.

◆ HABER PROCESS
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

◆ OSTWALD PROCESS
4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O
2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂
3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO

◆ CONTACT PROCESS
S + O₂ → SO₂
2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃
SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇
H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

◆ CHLOR-ALKALI PROCESS
2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂

◆ LIMESTONE DECOMPOSITION
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

◆ FERMENTATION
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

◆ SOAP FORMATION
Fat/Oil + NaOH → Soap + Glycerol

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ A good industrial process aims for high production, good product quality, efficient use of raw materials and energy, reasonable cost, safe operation, recycling of useful materials, and minimum environmental pollution.
